doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Art versus commerce and serious music
summary: Carter says art and commercial success can coexist and jokes about the green muse.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: What about the word serious? They were always talking about “serious music.”

Well, that has no meaning, because I think every . . . you know, the guy that plays a harmonica, and I don’t mean like Toots Tillman [phonetic], I mean just the guy who plays the harmonica in a blues thing or something. I don’t know what . . . where are we? [laughter] What was your question again?
Jeez, I think I’ve lost it again. No, the idea of art versus commerce in music, I think that’s sort of what we’re nudging towards.

Yes, art versus commerce, or art versus commercialism, maybe, or something. I don’t know. They can be different, and they can be the same. They can occur together, you know. But how to analyze and separate the two, I couldn’t just right at this moment do it off the top of my head unless I had time to do a dissertation. But yeah, I know what you mean.
For example . . . you were going to say something. Go ahead.

Well, I was going to say that, speaking of artists and commercialism, gee, how do artists become multimillionaires if they’re not commercial? You know, but the fact that you make a lot of money doesn’t mean that you’re not an artist if you’re commercial, you know.

I guess the differentiation might be that somebody is changing his art or doing something in order to make money, as opposed to just doing whatever it is that the muse leads him to do and it happens to sell as well. Just off the top of my head.

Well, the muse, what’s the color of the muse, green? [laughter] Okay, you know what the green muse is, the almighty American dollar. There’s nothing wrong with going after that, because that’s our society and what it’s really built on.
But obviously you, if it wasn’t a formal line that you drew, there was some kind of . . . there were some things you wouldn’t do. Let’s put it that way.
And an addition to that is there are some things I couldn’t do, you know, of which I’m fully aware and have always been. [Berger laughs.] Were you going to say, “Such as?”
Well, I was going to just cite one example, something that is . . . I don’t know what it means, exactly, but maybe I’ll throw it out to you and you can tell me what it means, if anything.
I can throw it back, huh?
